OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri K.V. Raghunatha Reddy, former Member of this House. 
Shri K..V. Raghunath Reddy passed away on 4th March, 2002 in New Delhi 
at the age of 78. 
Bom at Virur in Nellore district of Andhra Pradesh in September, 1924, Shri 
Reddy had his education at Annamalai University and Lucknow University. An 
advocate by profession, Shri Reddy was connected with the Afro-Asian Society 
and Peace Conference. 
Shri Raghunatha Reddy represented the State of Andhra Pradesh in this 
House for three consecutive terms from April, 1962 to April, 1968; from April, 
1968 to April, 1974; and again from April, 1974 to April, 1980. 
He served as Union Minister of State for Industrial Development and 
Company Affairs from 1967 to 1970 and Union Minister of Company Affairs 
from June, 1970 to February, 1973. From February, 1973 to November, 1973, 
Shri Reddy was Union Minister of Labour and Rehabilitation; and from 
November, 1973 to March, 1977 he held the portfolio of Labour Minister. He 
served as the Governor of Triupra from 1990 to 1993 and of West Bengal from 
1993 to 1998. 
Shri Reddy led the Indian Delegation to the Fifty-eighth, Fifty-ninth and 
Sixtieth Sessions of the International Labour Conference. He represented Rajya 
Sabha at the Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference held in London in June, 
1966. 
In the passing away of Shri K.V. Raghunatha Reddy, the country has lost 
an eminent parliamentarian and an able administrator.

Award of excellence relating to labour 
*107. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the criteria of selection for the "Shram Ratna. Shram Bhushan and 
Shram Vir" awards of excelcnce relating to labour; 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
(b) the content of such awards; 
(c) when these awards were established and since then how many have 
been awarded these awards, category-wise; 
(d) whether it is a fact that BHEL employees have got it for the last 
sixteen consecutive years; and 
(e) the composition of the Committee for selection of such awards? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (e) 
The Prime Minister's Shram Awards were established in the year 1985. 
These awards are presented to the workmen (as defined in the Industrial 
Dispute Act, 1947) employed in the Departmental Undertakings of the Central 
and State Governments and Central and State Public Sector Undertakings and 
engaged in manufacturing and productive processes and whose performance 
is assessable. Workmen solely engaged in routine service duties are not eligible. 
These awards are given to workmen who have a distinguished record of 
performance, devotion to duty of a high order, specific contribution in the 
field of productivity, proven innovativ e abilities, presence of mind and 
exceptional courage. The awards may be given to those workmen also who 
have made the supreme sacrifice of laying down their lives in the conscientious 
discharge of their duties. Adequate representation is given to women 
handicapped workers. The awards in the order of precedence are as under:— 
SHRAM RATNA being the highest award goes to a worker of really 
outstanding calibre. There is only one award in this category and carries a 
cash prize of Rs. 2,00,000/-. 
SHRAM BHUSHAN is awarded to workers who have made exceptional 
contribution in productivity/production and have also shown innovative abilities 
of high order. This category of awards are 2 in number and carries a cash prize 
each of Rs. 1,00,000/-. 
SHRAM VIR is awarded to workers who have a continuous record of 
dedicated service and high order of productivity. This category of awards are 6 
in number and carries a cash prize each of Rs. 60,000/-. 
SHRAM SHRI/SHRAM DEVI is awarded to workers who have shown 
exceptional zeal and enthusiasm for work and have had significant contribution 
16

towards productivity. This category of awards are 8 in number and carries a cash 
prize each of Rs. 40,000/-. 
Besides the cash prize, awardees also receive a "SAN AD" 
The Screening Committee consists of Secretary (Labour) as Chairman and 
an officer not below the level of Joint Secretary each from Prime Minister's 
Office, Cabinet Secretariat Ministry of Home Affairs and Department of Public 
Enterprises. 
It is not true that the BHEL employees have been awarded the Prime 
Minister's Shram Awards in the last sixteen consecutive years. The BHEL 
employees have not received the award for the year 2001. However, BHEL 
employees working in their different units in the country have been awarded 
from the year 1985 to 2000 consecutively.

Increase in unemployment 
*108.    SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that unemployment is gradually increasing in the 
country; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; 
(c) what steps are being taken to wipe out unemployment; and 
(d) how many persons were registered with various employment exchanges 
in the years 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and so far in 2002 for employment? 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (d) 
As per the Labour Force Survey conducted by National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO) during the year 1993-94 and 1999- 2000, the number of 
unemployed persons has marginally gone up from around 75 lakh in 1993-94 
to 90 lakh in 1999-2000 as per Usual Status Approach. The main reason for 
increase in the unemployed persons was that the economy did not grow at the 
desired rate to provide employment opportunties to all the new entrants to the 
labour force and the backlog of the unemployed. 
The approach to the Tenth Plan focusses on providing gainful high quality 
employment to the additions to the labour force and it is listed as one of the 
monitorable objectives for the 10th Plan and beyond. The growth strategy of 
the 10th Plan would lay emphasis on rapid growth of those sectors which are 
likely to create high quality employment opportunities and deal with the policy 
constraints which discourage growth of employment. Particular attention would 
be paid to the policy environment influencing a wide range of economic 
activities which have a large employment potential. 
The total number of job seekers, all of whom are not necessarily 
unemployed, registered with various Employment Exchanges in the country 
during the years (January to December) 1999, 2000 and 2001 were 59.7, 60.4 
and 55.5 lakh respectively.

* 112.    SHRIBHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
SHRIRAJUPARMAR: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have finalised a key anti-terrorist project titled 
Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (CCIT) and presented 
it before the United Nations recently; 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) the countries that have supported the Indian Government on this 
proposal and in what way it would help Government to curb terrorism? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to  (c) India circulated the draft 
Comprehensive Convention on Internat ional Terrorism (CCIT) at the UN 
General Assembly (UNGA) in 1996. The objective of the CCIT is to strengthen 
cooperation to combat international terrorism. 
The salient features of the CCIT, inter alia are: 
(i) all States have a responsibility not to support terrorist acts and/or to 
provide any assistance, training, safe haven etc.; 
00 all States should adopt measures to ensure that terrorist acts within 
the scope of the Convention are, under no circumstances, justified 
by considerations of political, philosophical, ideological, racial, 
religious or other similar nature; 
(iii) all States should take all practicable measures to prohibit the 
establishment and operation of terrorist installations and training 
camps; 
(iv)   terrorists should either be prosecuted or extradited. 
Four rounds of negotiations on the CCIT have taken place so far. It now 
enjoys wide support. Agreement has been reached on most aspects of the CCIT. 
Negotiations are continuing. 
The Convention, by providing a comprehensive legal framework, will 
help combat international terrorism.

comer notices against them; and

so far on Pakistan if it is not willing to follow the example of the United Arab 
Emirates for handing over such terrorists to India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) On 31st December 2001, 
Government handed' over t& Pakistan a consolidated list of 20 fugitives from 
law who have given safe haven in Pakistan. Government asked the Pakistani 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
authorities to apprehend and hand them over they could be brought to justice 
for the crimes committed in India. On 11th February 2002, India reiterated this 
demand, and also pointed out to Pakistan that the authorities of the United Arab 
Emirates (UAE), acting as per current international norms, deported to India two 
individuals responsible for the attack on the American Cultural Center in Kolkatta. 
The UAE authorities had not insisted upon time-consuming procedures of 
extradition, which which was very much in keeping with the requirements of the 
international campaign against terrorism. 
Government have indicated to Pakistan that of the 20 fugitives from law 
that figure on the list handed over to Pakistan on 31st December 2001, 15 
individuals have Interpol Red Comer notices issued them. This provides 
sufficient basis for Pakistan to take action. It is well known that according to 
Interpol norms, resolutions, decisions and procedures red notices are documents 
intended for both the police and the judicial authorities and can be considered 
valid requests for provision! arrest, because they are only issued on the basis 
of valid national warrants. Pakistan can also take action under a bilateral 
cooperative arrangement, which had been arrived at in 1989 by the Director-
CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) in India and Pakistan's Director General-
FIA (Federal Investigation Agency). Under this arrangement both agencies 
act as nodal agencies in their respective countries, to locate and trace out 
fugitives from law, and to arrange handing over of such wanted and absconding 
criminals to their respective counterpart without going through cumbersome 
and time-consuming procedures. 
Government are firmly resolved to continue taking all measures necessary 
to defeat Pakistan's sponsorship of cross border terrorism in India This includes, 
appropriately and effectively, highlighting to the international community is 
pertaining to Pakistan's continued sponsorship of cross border terrorism. India has 
received widespread support for its strong determination to resist terrorism unit it 
is decisively crushed The consensus in the intematonal community is that there is 
no justification for terrorism, which must be eradicated wherever it exists.

PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (f) The High Powered Committee on sugar industry recommended, inter-
aiia, decontrol of sugar. The recommendations of the Committee relating to 
decontrol of sugar and the gist of the Government decision thereon are indicated 
below:— 
Recommendation Nos. 3 to 6 
Recommendation No. 3: The Committee recommends complete decontrol of 
sugar, decontrol may, however, be phased over a period of two years. From the 
beginning of the Sugar Season following the date of announcement of the policy, the 
percentage of levy sugar may be reduced to 20% which may be continued at the same 
rate during the next Sugar Season and from the beginning of the subsequent Sugar 
Season the levy may be completely abolished. 
Recommendation No. 5: Spply of sugar through PDS may be discontinued 
when complete decontrol becomes effective. The subsidy at present allowed in 
supply of sugar through PDS can be distributed among the beneficiaries by adding to 
the subsidy at present allowed on foodgrains. 
Recommendation No. 6: If Government wishes to continue sugar under PDS, the 
required quantity may be purchased from industry/trade by tendering or at fixed prices 
from the Mills. Additional subsidy outgo would be offset by higher excise collection 
on levy quota converted as free sale. If shortfalls still continue, the balance may be 
met by increasing excise duty to the required level. 
Gist of decision on Recommendation Nos. 3,5 and 6: 
"Government has already reduced the percentage of levy sugar from 40% to 
30% with effect from 1.1.2000. Government cannot agree on any time frame for 
further decontrol as recommended by the Committee as this depends upon the 
restructuring of the PDS of which sugar is an essential part Further reduction of levy 
percentage and alternative methods of meeting the requirement for distribution of sugar 
under the PDS are all linked to the restructuring of PDS." 
Recommendation No. 4: Control on releases should continue even after 
complete decontrol of prices. 
Gist of decision on Recommendation No. 4: 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
"The Mahajan Committee has made a distinction between decontrol of 
the sugar industry and decontrol of prices, the latter being restricted to the 
system of levy obligation from the sugar mills. Government does not accept 
the recommendation that control on releases should continue without any time 
limit. Government is committed to phased decontrol of sugar industry and that 
the process of phased decontrol will have to be effected in a manner so as to 
avoid any destabilization of the sugar industry and the prices and should be 
accompanied by a number of steps including establishment of a foward/future 
market for sugar to achieve long term price stabilization." 
In the light of the above decisions of the Government, the levy obligation, 
which was reduced from 40% to 30% with effect from 1.1.2000, has been further 
reduced to 15% and 10% with effect from 1.2.2001 and 1.3.2002 respectively. 
Now, the Government has decided to effect complete decontrol of sugar after 
operationalisation of futures/forward trading in 2002-2003 financial year.

Failure of PDS 
818. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of CON-
SUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the PDS has failed in the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such failure and the steps taken or proposed to 
take to improve PDS in the country; 
(c) whether Government are thinking of alternative income generating 
schemes for the poor in place of PDS; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN) 
(a) and (b) No, Sir, The Public Distribution system (PDS) is one of the important 
elements of the Government's food security system in the country. 
The PDS is the joint responsibility of the Central Government and the 
State Govemments/UT Administrations. The Central Government is responsi-
ble for procuring, storing and transporting PDS commodities upto the Central 
godowns and making them available to the States/UTs actual distribution of 
PDS commodities through Fair Price Shops is the responsibility of the State 
Governments /UTs Administrations. 
Some shortcomings in a vast system of public distribution of subsidized 
commodities cannot be ruled out altogether. In order to make the PDS more effec-
tive, efficient and accountable, the Government has issued the Public Distribution 
system (Control) Order, 2001 under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 
1955. The salient features of the Order relate to proper identification of eligible 
families, issue of ration cards, licensing of fair shops, scale of issue and issue 
prices, distribution of essential commodities and monitoring. Any contravention 
of the provisions of clauses 3,4,6 and 7 of the Order is liable for criminal punish-
ment under section 7 of the Essential Commoditis Act, 1955. 
The Government has advised the State Govemments/UT Administrations 
to involve the Gram Panchayats more substantially in the supervision and moni-
toring of the PDS, especially at the FPS levele, as a measure of social audit. A 
Model Citizens' Charter has also been drawn and circulated to States/UTs for 
adoption. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
(c) and (d) No such proposal to replace the PDS is under consideration at 
present. However, the Government has launched many schemes, including em-
ployment generating schemes, for the welfare of the poor.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject: Local purchase of stationery and other articles from the Central 
Government Employees Consumer Co-operative Society Limited, New Delhi. 
The undersigned is directed to re fer to this Department's Office 
Memorandum No. 14/14/80- Welfare dated the 20th June, 1980, on the subject 
mentioned above in which it was stated that all local purchases of official 
requirements of articles of stationery, sanitary, electrical and other items be 
made through the Central Government Employees Consumer Co-operative 
Society Limited, New Delhi without going through the eleborate procedure of 
calling for quotations and / or rate list. Subse quently, it was clarified vide this 
Department's Office Memorandum of even number dated the 16th May, 1981 
that while purchase upto Rs. 250/- can be made from the Co-operative Society 
without calling for tenders, where purchases are in excess of this limit, the 
provisions of the General Financial rules will apply and tenders are to be in-
vited as laid down in chapter 8 of the General Financial rules, 1963. 
2. The matter has since been reviewed. It is one of the avowed objectives 
of the cooperative movement to ensure supply of goods and services to the 
consumers at the most economical and competitive prices. Taking note of this 
commitment, the Department of Cooperation had issued general guidelines as 
early as 1968 to all State Governments and Union Territories to the effect that 
Government offices should patronize consumer cooperative stores while mak-
ing purchases of their requirements. This was reterated in another circular 
letter addressed to all State Governments etc. in March, 1972, by the Depart-
ment of Cooperation. It has been stated in that letter that consumer coopera-
tives, especially departmental stores, which have received substantial finan-
cial assistance from Government and are subject to statutory supervision and 
control by the registrars of Cooperative Societies and State Governments are 
the most suitable agencies for supply of consumer goods at fair and reason- 
130 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
able prices and that while rendering honest and efficient service, their dealings 
are free from malpractices often indulged in by private traders such as profiteering, 
adulteration, sale of spurious and sub-standard goods, underweighment and tax 
evasion. This Department, therefore, felt that there was no reason why guide-
lines issued by the Central Government to State Governments and Union Terri-
tories should not be made applicable to the Central Government Departments in 
the matter of purchases made by them. 
3. The Central Government Employees Consumer Cooperative Society 
Limited, New Delhi, which was set up in 1963 as a well measure to provide 
articles of daily necessities to Government employees at reasonable prices, 
functions under the supervision and control of the Department of Personnel & 
A.R. Besides substantial investments made in the share capital of the Society, 
the Government have been providing financial assistance to it from time to 
time by way of subsidy, loans, cellateral guarantee against borrowings etc. The 
Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Society is a Joint Secretary of the 
Department of Personnel & A.R. who exercises direct and close control over its 
activities. 
4. Keeping the background set out in paragraph 2 and 3 above, the Min-
istry of Works & Housing and Department of Supply who were consulted, have 
agreed that it may be made incumbent on all Central Government Departments, 
their attached and subordinate offices and other organizations financed and / 
or controlled by the Government located at Delhi / New Delhi to make all local 
purchases of stationery and other items required by them only from the Central 
Government Employees Consumer Cooperative Society Limited, New Delhi. Only 
if the society is not able to supply, a particular item, will it be permissible for them 
to make local purchase from other sources. 
5. The prices-of the various articles sold through the outlets of this Society 
are, by and large, less than obtaining in the market. Keeping this aspect in view, 
the Ministry of Finance have agreed to waive the procedure laid down in chapter 
8 of the General Financial rules regarding calling of tenders for such purchases as 
are made from the Central Government Consumer Co-operative Society Limited. 
However, with a view to provide a safeguard for ensuring quality as well as fair 
price, it has been decided that articles as are generally intended for by Govern-
ment Departments etc. will be fixed by a Committee consisting of a representa-
tive each of the Department of Supply, Works and Housing and the Central 
Government Employees Consumer Cooperative Society and the prices so fixed

will remain in force for a period of three months. The General Manager of the

articles available with the Society.

may kindly be noted carefully and complied with in a respect of local purchases to 
be made by Government Departments etc., hereafter, Ministries / Departments are 
also requested to instruct their attached and subordinate offices as well as 
autonomous bodies and public sector undertakings under their control to allow the 
same procedure for obtaining their requirements of stationery and other items from 
the society.

New Delhi, the 28th February, 2002 
OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Sub:   Special Voluntary Retirement Scheme for Surplus Central Govern-
ment Employees. 
The Expenditure Reforms Commission (ERC) set up by the Government of 
India has suggested a liberal Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) for the 
employees declared surplus. This recommendation, contained in Commission's 
second Report on "Optimising Government's Staff Strength—Some General 
Issues" has been considered carefully and the Central Government have decided 
to introduce a special Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) as per details given in 
para 2 hereinunder for-the permanent employees declared surplus in any 
Ministry/Department as a consequence of one or more of the following:*- 
140 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Ministry/Department as a consequence of one or more of the fol lowing: - 
(i) Implementation of decisions of the Cabinet regarding restructuring 
of Ministries/Departments; 
(ii) Implementation of the recommendations of the Expenditure Reforms 
Commission; 
(iii) Implementation of the decision of a Ministry/Department relating to 
downsizing/rightsizing including, inter alia, restructuring of an or-
ganization, transfer of an activity to a State Government, Public 
Sector Undertaking or other Autonomous Organisation, discon-
tinuation of an ongoing activity and introduction of changes in 
technology; or 
(iv) implementation of work study reports undertaken by the Staff In-
spection Unit of the Ministry of Finance or any other body set up 
by the Central Government or the Ministry/Department concerned. 
2. The features of the Special VRS for the employees declared surplus are 
as under :- 
(a) All permanent employees rendered surplus irrespective of their age 
and qualifying service can opt for the scheme. 
(b) An optee of Special VRS will be entitled to receive an ex-graf/aamount 
equal to basic pay plus deamess allowance for the number of days worked out 
on the basis of length of service @35 days for each completed year and 25 days 
for each remaining year. For any part of a year, the number of days, for ex-gratia 
amount, will be worked out on the basis of 365 days in a year. The ex-gratia 
amount will be further subject to the following conditions: 
(i) Total number of years to be counted for payment of ex-gratia will 
not exceed 33 years; 
(ii) No weightage of additional service will be given for the purpose of 
calculation of ex-gratia; 
(iii) The ex-gratia will be subject to a minimum of Rs.25,000/- or 250 
days emoluments, whichever is higher; 
(iv) The ex-gratia amount should not exceed the sum of the basic pay 
plus DA that the employee would draw at the prevailing level for 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
the balance of the period of service left before superannuation; 
(v)     The ex-gratia amount will be paid in lump-sum; 
(vi) The ex-gratia amount up to Rs.5.00 lakhs will be exempted from 
Income Tax; 
(c) A weightage of five years to the qualifying service shall be given 
under CCS(Pension) Rules, 1972 to such permanent surplus 
employees who have rendered a minimum of 15 years of qualifying 
service on the date they are declared surplus. However, as provided 
in rule 29 of CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972, the qualifying length of 
service after taking into account the aforesaid weightage should 
not be more than the service he would have rendered had he retired 
on the date of his superannuation. 
(d) Encashment of Earned Leave accumulated on the date of relief as 
per CCS(Leave) Rules, 1972; 
(e) Payment of savings element with interest in the Central Government 
employees Group Insurance Scheme as per rules; 
(f) TA/DA as on retirement for self and family for settling anywhere in 
India as per Travelling Allowance Rules; 
(g) Group "A" officials opting for the special VRS will be exempted from 
the operation of rule 10 of the CCS (Pension) Rules which stipulates 
previous sanction of the Government for accepting commercial em-
ployment. 
 
3. Payment of ex-gratia to the employees declared surplus and opting 
for the special VRS within the specified three months period will be over 
and above the normal retirement entitlements under CCS (Pension) Rules, 
1972. 
4. The order of voluntary retirement in each case should clearly 
stipulate that the surplus post held by the retiring incumbent will stand 
abolished from the date of his/her voluntary retirement. 
5. The identification of surplus employees for the purpose of VRS 
would be guided by procedure given in Item 3 of Annexure-I under the 
heading "Steps for identification of Surplus staff' to the revised scheme of 
the disposal 6f personnel rendered surplus due to reduction of establishment 
in Central

Government Department/Offices notified vide Circular No. 1/18/88-CS-III of DoPT

Financial condition of States 
880. SHRISURESH PACHOURI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether finances of the State Governments have deteriorated since 1998; 
(b) if so, the details of the various aspects of this deterioration; and 
(c) the details of measures taken by Central and State Governments to 
improve the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUDHARA RAJE): (a) to (c) Finances of the State Governments 
have generally deteriorated since 1997 mainly due to the upward revision of sala-
ries of the State Government employees. The relatively stagnant revenues of the 
State.Governments forced them to depend more and more on borrowed funds. 
The Financial Management of the States is primarily the responsibility of 
the State Governments and it is for the respective State Governments to initiate 
remedial action. However, in order to alleviate the mismatch in the States' cash 
flow, the Government of India releases plan assistance, share in Central taxes and 
small savings loans in advance depending on the need and request of the State 
Government. In addition to Ways and Means support by Reserve Bank of India, 
Central Government also provides Way and Means advance to States. 
Pursuant to the recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission, a 
scheme for the States' Fiscal Reform Facility has been drawn up by the Government 
of India. Under the scheme, States have been encouraged to draw up a monitorable 
fiscal reforms programme aimed at improving their financial position in the medium 
term. Incentive funds will be made available to States periodically depending on 
the progress in achieving fiscal reform targets.

 48. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY

machines used to carry out sex determination tests not even a single machine

Bhopal gas tragedy after-effects 
*53. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state; 
(a) whether in 17 years since the Bhopal Gas Tragedy happened it has 
now been revealed by a Fact-Finding Mission that toxic chemicals from the 
Union Carbide Factory have spread not only into soil, water and vegetables 
but even inside breast milk; 
(b) whether it is a fact that these toxins are now being passed on from 
mothers to their children and have shown a dangerous pattern of mental health 
illness specific to Bhopal survivors; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government are taking to check any such incident in 
future? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Government of India is aware that a Non-Governmental 
Fact-Finding Mission has very recently gone into the possibility of toxic 
chemicals from the Union Carbide factory spreading into the soil, water and 
vegetables. However, no comments can be offered on the report until the same is 
considered by the technical agencies within the Government. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
However, the Government of Madhya Pradesh have intimated that they 
are not aware of any such study conducted in this regard. There are some 
hazardous chemicals still lying in the factory and the Government of Madhya 
Pradesh is taking steps to safely dispose of the same in consultation with the 
Defence Research Development Organisation (DRDO). 
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) had conducted a study 
in 1985 on the genetic risks evaluation of pregnancy outcome in pregnant 
women exposed to toxic gas and to monitor the teratogenic potential of the 
toxic gas on the outcome and development of new boms delivered by the 
exposed mothers. Information obtained on 2566 women who were pregnant at 
the time of exposure and who were followed up, revealed that while abortion 
rates were higher than the national average, perinatal mortality rates were 
within the limit. There was also no increase in the occurrence of congenital 
malformation. Another study conducted by the ICMR was on the prevalence 
of psychiatric morbidity in the area, and it reveals that the prevalence rate was 
higher in the exposed areas as compared to the controlled areas which showed 
decreasing trend with time.

Health care centres for mentally challenged persons 
*58.  DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that under the provisions of Mental Health Act, 
1987, Government have to set-up at least one health care centres for the 
mentally challenged persons in the States; 
(b) the number of centres, so far, set-up in the States; and 
(c) whether Government propose to increase their number in view of 
the deplorable conditions in some private mental asylums? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.R 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Mental Health Act, 1987, provides that "The Central 
Government may, in any part of India, or the State Government may, within 
the limits of its jurisdiction, establish or maintain psychiatric hospitals or 
psychiatric nursing homes for the admission, treatment and care of mentally 
202 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
ill persons at such places as it thinks fit." The State/Central Government, 
therefore, decide in the matter keeping in view the disease burden and other 
connected issues. 
The present policy of the Government is to strengthen the infrastructural 
facilities and services in the existing mental hospital/institutions in order to 
maximize the benefits to the mentally ill persons, rather than create new 
infrastructure, at this stage. At present, there are 40 Mental Health Care 
institutions in the Public Sector which includes Central Government institutes 
like NIMHANS and CIP, Ranchi. 
The aim of the Government is to identify persons suffering from various 
mental disorders and epilepsy and manage them at the primary health care 
centre and district level by trained doctors and with the active support of the 
families and the community in which the patient lives. Towards this aim, 
District Mental Health Programme has already been initiated under the National 
Mental Health Programme and is presently being implemented in 25 districts 
covering 20 States and Union Territories in the country.

Malnutrition and related diseases 
346. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that malnutrition problem and related diseases 
are increasing in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to eradicate such problems? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) The malnutrition levels in the 
country are not increasing but have been gradually reducing as per the facts 
given below: 
(i) Protein energy malnutrition in the children has been reduced from 
68.6% in 1988—90 to 47% in 1998-99. 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
(ii) Vitamin-A deficiency as indicated by Bitot spot has reduced from 
1.8% in children during the year 1975-79 to 1.1% in the year 1994-
95. 
(iii)   Prevalence to goitre has reduced from 21.0% in 1989 to 10% in 1994. 
(iv) Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women has reduced from 87.5% 
in 1989 to 84.9% in 1999. 
(v) Chronic energy deficiency in adults has reduced from 5.1.8% in 
females and 55.6% in males in 1975—79 to 36.3% in females and 
28.6% in males in the year 1995-96. 
(c) The Government of India adopted the National Nutrition Policy in 
1993 which advocated a multisectoral approach for controlling the problem 
of malnutrition and improving nutritional status of the people. The National 
Nutritional Policy contains both short term/direct interventions and long 
term/indirect interventions. A National Plan of Action on Nutrition was 
developed to serve as a frame-work for translating the instruments of National 
Nutrition Policy which identified the role of 14 Departments/Ministries of the 
Government towards nutrition promotion. 
Various measures adopted by the Government to improve the nutritional 
status of the population are:— 
(i) Increased agricultural production; 
(ii) Improving the purchasing power of the people through income 
generating schemes; 
(iii) Availability of essential food items at subsided cost through public 
distribution system; 
(iv) Nutrition education to increase the awareness and bringing about the 
desired changes in the feeding practices including promotion of breast 
feeding; 
(v) Supplementary feeding programmes viz (a) Integrated Child 
Development Services (ICDS) schemes; (b) Special Nutrition 
Programme (SNP); (c) Balwadi Nutrition Programme (BNP); (d) 
Wheat Based Supplementary Nutrition Programme; (e) Mid-Day 
Meal Programme; (0 Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY); 
(g) Programmes for prevention of specific nutrient deficiency disorders 
256 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
such as National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme; 
Prophylaxis Programme as to prevent blindness due to Vitamin-A 
deficiency and Nutritional Anaemia due to Iron Deficiency as a part 
of Reproductive and Child Health Programme; Pilot Project for control 
of micro-nutrient malnutrition is also under implementation.

Illegal foetus testing machines 
351. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many foetus testing machines are being 
operated without any licence; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to take any specific steps 
to check this; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Sex of the foetus can be 
detected by various methods. The ultrasound machines/scanners/imaging 
machines are most commonly used for this purpose. The Pre-natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 prohibits 
determination and disclosure of sex of the foetus. Clinics using pre-natal 
diagnostic techniques like ultrasound machines are required to get themselves 
registered under the Act so as to discourage and discontinue their use for 
detection of sex of the foetus during pregnancy. A large number of clinics/ 
institutes using such machines are not registered under this Act taking the 
plea that they are not using these machines for detection of sex of foetus.

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
However, there is nothing to confirm that they are not actually doing so. 
Accordingly, the Supreme Court of India in its Order dated 11 th December, 
2001 had directed that information relating to buyers of ultrasound machines 
may be obtained from the manufacturers, importers, suppliers etc. of such 
machines. 
A list of over 11,000 buyers of u ltrasound machines received from the 
suppliers has already been passed on to the States/UTs for ensuring the 
registration of clinics at the addresses cited under the said PNDT Act, and for 
prosecution of those who may be found misusing these machines for detection 
of sex of foetus. 
In a subsequent order dated 29th January, 2002 the Supreme Court has 
directed the sealing and seizure of ultrasound machines/scanners used by 
organizations not registered under the said Act All the States and UTs have 
been advised to take immediate necessary steps to implement these directives.

Incentives to states achieving the targets under population control 
programme 
†367. SHRI KR1PAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pelased to state: 
(a) the details of the States which are achieving targets set under 
Population Control Programme sponsored by Government; 
(b) whether any assistance or incentive is exchanged to these States for 
achieving the targets; and 
(c) if so, the details of the assistance extended to these States during the 
last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) There has been a paradigm 
shift in the Family Welfare Programme under which fixing of targets has been 
abandoned. Instead the 'Target Free Approach (TFA)' was adopted since 1st 
April 1996 all over India and the system of decentralized participatory planning 
is brought in place. TFA has been renamed as Community Needs Assessment 
Approach (CNAA) from 1997. Under the new approach i.e. CNAA attention 
is being paid towards providing quality of care in aspect of basic and essential 
family welfare services. This serves to shift the emphasis from quantitative or 
numerical targets in the achievement of family planning acceptance to the  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
276 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
qualitative aspect of integrated service delivery. Another important aspect of 
the new approach is to ensure community participation in the implementation 
of the Family Welfare Programme at the grass-root level. 
Since October, 1997 Government of India (Department of Family 
Welfare) has introduced Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme 
which is being implemented under the new approach i.e. decentralized 
participatory planning under which annual action plan is oriented from the 
grass root level giving adequate attention to the care of health of pregnant 
women, infants and children including acceptance of contraceptive method 
according to voluntary choice for using any method. 
The requirement of Total Fertility rate (average number of children per 
couple) of'2.1 towards achieving population stabilisation has already been 
achieve in 9 States and Union Territories. They are Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Goa, 
Nagland, Delhi, Pondicherry, A & N Island, Chandigarh and Mizoram. 
The 12 States and Union Territories which have total fertility rate of 
more than 2.1 but less than 3.0 are Kamataka, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, 
Maharashtra, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Orissa, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, 
Lakshdweep, Daman and Diu and Sikkim. Many of these States have made 
strenuous efforts to improve their indicators in respect of fertility regulation. 
There are 11 States and Union Territories that have total fertility rate of 
over 3. They are Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Assam, 
Haryana, Gujarat, Tripura, Meghalaya, Jammu & Kashmir, Dadra and Nagar 
Haveli. 
No special assistance or incentive is extended to the states performing 
better.However, due to better performance under various family welfare 
schemes they get more funds for those schemes. Further, in order that the 
Governments persue the agenda for population stabilisation, the number of 
representatives in the Lok Sabha has be en frozen till 2026 at the population 
level of census 1971, through Constitution (91st Amendment) Bill passed by 
Parliament in August 2001.

Powers to Lok Adalats 
402. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to give more powers to Lok Adalats 
in view of their better performance in the past; 
(b) if so, whether Government are proposing to introduce a Bill to enlarge 
the Lok Adalats; 
(c) if so, the details of the same; 
(d) the total number of Lok Adalats to be set up in each State; 
(e) the power to be provided to them; and 
(f) to what extent it will reduce the cases pending with the various courts 
in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. At present, the Lok Adalats can 
settle disputes only on the basis of compromise or settlement among the parties. 
If the parties do not arrive at a settlement, the case is either returned to the court 
of law or the parties are advised to seek remedy in a court of law. To remove 
this drawback, it has been decided to add a new Chapter in the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987, which will facilitate setting up of permanent Lok Adalats 
314 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
for providing compulsory pre-litigative mechanism for conciliation and 
settlement of cases relating to public utility services. 
(d) The National Legal Services Authority or the State Legal Services 
Authority, as the case may be, may establish permanent Lok Adalat at such 
places and in such numbers as may be expedient to enable the Lok Adalats to 
exercise its jurisdiction in respect of one or more public utility services as 
necessary from time to time. 
(e) The permanent Lok Adalats would have jurisdiction regarding public 
utittty services such as transport (air, road, water), postal, telegraph or telephone, 
power, water, sanitation, hospitals and insurance. To avoid prolonged litigation 
it has also been proposed that the award made by the Lok Adalat shall be final, 
binding and shall not be questioned in any original suit, application or execution 
proceeding. The jurisdiction of the Lok Adalats would, however, be limited to 
cases upto a monetary value of Rs. 10 lakhs. 
(f) It is not possible to quantify the reduction in the Court cases at present.

of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state:

country adoption of children till new guidelines are formulated to safeguard the 
interests of adopted children; 
(b) whether certain cases have come to light where prospective adoptive 
parents are having dubious record, all sorts of physical ailments, two or more 
children, and are divorcee lesbian and overaged; and

are protected? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) No request has been received by the Ministry 
from any State Government or organization to stop inter-country adoption of 
children.

in which it has referred to allegations that children have been given without 
verifying the background and financial stability of the persons adopting. The 
Ministry has also received copy of a letter sent by an NGO to the National 
Human Rights Commission about alleged unsuitability of some foreign nationals 
adopting Indian children. 
(c) Inter-country adoptions are governed by the Revised Guidelines for 
Adoption of Indian Children, 1995, which are reviewed from time to time as 
and when necessary. No direct adoption of children is permitted. Adoption is 
done through licensed agencies both in country and abroad.

Urban Poor in Andhra Pradesh 
440. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister 
of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the number of percentage of urban poor in Andhra Pradesh as on date; 
(b) the latest definition of urban poor and economic criteria therefor; 
(c) whether the number of urban poor in Andhra Pradesh increased/ 
decreased during the last three years alongwith the details thereof, year-wise; 
(d) the steps taken by Government during the Ninth Plan period to 
eradicate the urban poverty in the State and progress achieved; and 
(e) the steps proposed to be taken to eradicate urban poverty in Andhra 
Pradesh during the Tenth Plan period? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Planning Commission have reported that based on the data 
from the latest large sample survey of the 55th round on consumer expenditure 
conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), the number and 
percentage of poor in urban area of Andhra Pradesh has been estimated as 60.88 
lakhs, which is 26.63 per cent of the total urban population in 1999-2000. 
(b) The Planning Commission has adopted per capita consumption 
expenditure as the criterion to determine poverty. In urban areas, the per capita 
consumption has been fixed at Rs. 56.64 per month at 1973-74 prices 
corresponding to a basket of goods and services anchored on a norm of per 
capita daily calorie requirement of 2100 Kcal in urban areas. 
(c) The Planning Commission estimates poverty at national and state level 
from the large sample survey on consumer expenditure conducted by the NSSO 
at an interval of approximately five years. The two latest such surveys were 
conducted in the years 1993-94 (NSS 50th Round and 1999-2000 (NSS 55th 
Round). As such, the estimates of poverty during the last three years are not 
available. However, the number of urban poor in Andhra Pradesh in 1993-94 
was estimated as 74.47 lakhs.

implementing Swama Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), a Centrally

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY AL LEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA) (a) to (c) Yes, Sir, Slum Development being a State subject, 
State Government survey and take stock of slum in their respective State. 
However, the Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) Conducted a 
one time study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report title. A 
Compendium on Indian slums-1996" and according to this report the identified/ 
estimated urban slum populations in the country for 1981, 1991 and 2001 was 
279. 144 lakhs, 462.608 lakhs and 618.258 lakhs respectively. 
As per Information furnished by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi as 
on January, 1990 there were about 2.59 lakh jhuggies comprising a population 
of approximately 13 lakhs which in 1994 increased to about 4.80 lakh jhuggies 
with approximately population of 20-22 lakhs. Thereafter no survey has been 
undertaken by them. Presently according to rough estimate, there are about 6 
lakh jhuggies comprising of about 30 lakh jhuggi dwellers in Delhi. 
However, with a view to ameliorate the living conditions of the slum 
dwellers, a scheme known as National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) 
has been in operation since 1996 to provide Additional Central Assistance to 
States/UTs for development of urban slums. Under NSDP, funds are allocated 
by the Planning Commission and released by Ministry of Finance. 
A New Scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas-Yojana (VAMBAY) has 
been announced by the Hon'ble Prime Minister on 15th August, 2001 for 
upgradation/relocation of dwelling units in urban slums with 50% Central 
Government subsidy & 50% contribution from State Government (or taken as 
loan by State from HUDCO/Financial Institutions/Banks etc.) The allocation 
under VAMBAY for current year 2001 -02 is Rs. 69.00 crores (Revised Estimates). 
To integrate sanitation as part of the housing development, a sub-
component namely Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan has also been launched under 
VAMBAY which will cater to Community Toilet Schemes. The percentage 
of funds for Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan would be 20% with a 5% additional 
component being kept for supporting infrastructure like drinking water/drainage 
etc. (total not to exceed 25% of VAMBAY outlay).

new scheme known as "Valmiki Ambe dkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY)' with 
the objective of providing shelter or upgrading the existing shelter for slum

Statement 
Initiatives taken by DDA towards zero tolerance corruption 
DDA have adopted three-pronged strategy viz. preventive, detective & 
punitive to curb corruption in the organization. To maintain integrity in the 
Department, instructions regarding anti-curruption measures issued by the 
Department of Personnel and Training and Ministry of Urban Development 
are being scrupulously followed. Measures for strengthening of Vigilanc 
Admn. & anti-corruption work as advised by the Central Vigilance Commission 
are also being implemented. 
Several long-term measures have been initiated by DDA to train its 
work force, introduced computerization and e-govemance as well as exercising 
strict vigilance at all levels. 
Various preventive measures have been taken to streamline the functioning 
of the organization i.e. monitoring/implementation of time limits provided for 
various items/transactions in DDA as pe r citizen's charter. The system of 
acknowledging letters & documents has been put in place. The Centralized 
Receipt & Despatch Section has been computerized and the public is issued a 
computerized acknowledgement against their letters. All important letters like 
demand-cum-allotment letters, refunds etc. are being sent by Speed Post and 
proof of delivery is being obtained from Post Office. 
13 Counsellors/Facilitators have been permanently seated in the main 
Reception Hall of Vikas Sadan for personally attending to the public visiting 
DDA offices for various transactions. These Counsellors apart from guidance 
also help in documentation. 
All the procedures are being further reviewed to minimize public 
complaints. 
Steps have been taken to disseminate information regarding functions and 
facilities provided by public dealing departments to customers by way of issuing 
brochures, hand books and notices in newspapers & public places. DDA has 
also created a Website (dda.delhi.com) to provide information to public. 
As a short-term measure, disciplinary action is being taken against 
defaulting officials. During the year 2001-2002, the departmental action has 
been initiated against 100 officials. During the same period, disciplinary cases

Water crisis 
†*66. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is likelihood of serious water crisis in 
the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government are contemplating to make any policy to 
deal with the same; and 
(c) if so, the outline thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) As per the latest  assessment made by Central Water 
Commission (CWC), the average annual water availability in the river systems 
of the country is assessed at 1869 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM). In 1951 with 
country's population of 361 millions, the per capita water availability was 5177 
cubic metre per year. Now, as per the population census of 2001 AD, the per 
capita water availability has come down to 1820 cubic metre per year. 
According to the international criteria, a situation of annual water 
availability of less than 1000 cubic metre per capita is considered as scarcity 
condition. However, it is estimated that due to increasing population, the 
average annual per capita water availability may further come down to about 
1341 cubic metre by 2025 AD and 1140 cubic metre by 2050 AD at the 
national level. However, due to the spatial variability of rain in the country 
and also because of variation in population density, per capita average annual 
availability of water in different basins presently varies from 13,636 cubic 
metre in Brahmaputra-Barak basin to 298 cubic metre in Sabarmati basin. 
This is likely to further accentuate in future and by 2050 AD, 71 percent of 
area covering 75 percent of the population will be facing water scarcity 
conditions. Further, the temporal variability in the rainfall also creates 
temporary scarcity of water in certain years. 
The National Water Policy adopted in 1987 does recognise that the water 
resources available to the country should be brought within the category of 
utilisable resources to the maximum possible extent. It lays emphasis on the 
conservation of the available resources and its augmentation by measures for 
maximising retention and minimising losses. Recycling and reuse of water are 
provided as integral parts of water resources development. Exploitation of 
ground water resources is directed to be so regulated as not to exceed the 
393 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
recharging possibilities, as also to ensure social equity. The policy also provides 
that ground water recharge projects should be developed and implemented for 
augmenting the available supplies and that the integrated and coordinated 
development of surface water and ground water and their conjunctive use 
should be envisaged right from the project planning stage. It recognises the 
need to make water available to water short areas by transfer from other areas 
including transfer from one river basin to another, based on a national 
perspective, after taking into account the requirements of the areas/basins. 
In order to meet the water demand for agricultural purposes, Government 
of India has been extend ing financial assistance un der Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefit Programme since 1996-97 to State Governments to help them complete 
the ongoing irrigation projects early. Government of India is also promoting 
rain water harvesting through Watershed Management Programme, artificial 
recharge of ground water and roof-top rain water harvesting under the sector 
reform project of Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme under the 
Ministry of Rural Development, for which technical and financial assistance 
is provided to the State Government and other implementing agencies. Central 
Ground Water Board has also taken up pilot studies for artificial recharge of 
ground water. For meeting future requirements of water, as a long term measure, 
National Water Development Agency have formulated National perspective 
Plan for water resources development which envisages interlinking between 
various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from surplus 
basins to water deficit basins.

As per the Budget Estimates prepared by the Company for the year 
2000-01 in December, 1999, Indian Airlines had projected a net profit of Rs. 
28.75 crores. Subsequent to the Budget approval in December, 1999, due to 
steep rise in various input costs, the Revised Estimate for the year 2000-2001 
reflected a net loss of Rs. 177.25 crores. The actual loss, as per the Annual 
Accounts for the year 2000-01 (provisional), is a lower net loss i.e. Rs. 159.17 
crores. The losses due to external factors and beyond the control of Indian 
Airlines were due to the following:— 
There were two successive hikes in Aviation Turbine Fuel prices during 
the year 2000, as a result of which the average price per kiloliter of Aviation 
Turbine Fuel (ATF) went up from Rs. 15,180/to Rs. 22,500/a staggering 
increase of around 48% resulting in an additional outgo of Rs. 231/crbres on 
Indian Airlines and Rs. 61/crores on Alliance Air, its subsidiary during the 
fiscal year 2000-01. 
In the aftermath of Kathmandu hijack in December, 1999, the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation decided that Sky Marshals should travel on security sensitive 
flights of Indian Airlines, and that Indian Airlines should bear this expenditure. 
Expenditure on this and other related security enhancement requirements has 
been Rs. 10/crores during 2000-01. During the period under review Sky Marshal 
did not travel on flights of any other scheduled domestic airlines. 
Ministry of Finance imposed a duty of 3% on import of aircraft, leased 
or purchased, which had an additional burden of Rs. 8/crores on import of two 
leased Airbus A-320 aircraft by Indian Airlines. 
Cochin has built a new private airpor t at Nedumbassery. Air India has 
been given the sole concessionaire rights from May, 1999 for handling flights 
of all airlines. Prior to this, Indian Airlines used to operate to the Naval airfield 
at Cochin where it used to handle its own flights. This change caused an 
additional outgo of Rs. 10/crores. 
In the aftermath of a hard landing of an A-320 aircraft at Yangon in 
October, 1999 hijack of Airbus A-300 from Kathmandu in December, 1999, 
and accident of Boeing 737 aircraft at Patna in July, 2000, the reinsurance 
market raised premium payments of Indian Airlines by USD 3 million (Rs. 14 
crores) in October, 2000. 
The exchange rate of one US dollar increased from Rs. 44/to 47/during 
the financial year 2000-01.

Capacity Production, in terms of Available Tonne Kilometers (ATKMs),

AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a afact that the European Union's new Generalised 
System of Preferences (GSP) that came into effect on January 1, 2002 would 
not be favourable to Indian exports; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the worst affected area for Indian exporters

INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The new

Declaration of TRIPS on Health Sector 
†489. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether declaration regarding Trade Related Intellectual Property 
Rights (TRIPS) and health have been issued in Doha conference of World Trade 
organisation despite all types of apprehensions; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 427 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what will be the effect of this declaration of Indian Drug Industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) to (c) Doha Declaration 
on the TRIPS Agreement on Public health affirms that the TRIPS Agreement 
can and should be interpreted to protect public health and promote access to 
medicines for all. The Declaration recognizes the affordability and 
availability of medicines as a universal right. The Ministers agreed that the 
TRIPS Agreement does not and should not prevent Members from taking 
measures to protect public health. The Declaration reaffirms the Members' 
right to use, to the full, the flexibility of compulsory license and parallel 
import for the purpose of public health. It clarifies that the Government have 
freedom to determine the grounds to grant compulsory licenses-. The 
Declaration also clarifies that each Member has the right to determine what 
constitutes a national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency 
for issuing compulsory license on an expeditious basis. The Declaration also 
clarifies that each Member is free to establish its own regime for exhaustion 
of IPRs. 
The Declaration recognizes the problem of countries with insufficient or no 
manufacturing capacities in the pharmaceutical sector in effectively using the 
flexibility of compulsory license and instructs the TRIPS Council to find an 
expeditious solution to this problem and to report to the GeneralCouncil before 
the end of 2002. The Declaration provides that the LDC Members will not be 
obliged, with respect to pharmaceutical products, to implement the provisions of 
the TRIPS Agreement relating to patent protection and undisclosed information 
until 1.1.2016. 
The Declaration would allow more flexible interpretation of the provisions 
of the TRIPS Agreement in undertaking measures to protect public health. The 
declaration clarifies the flexibilities available in the TRIPS Agreement relating 
to compulsory license and parallel import and removes ambiguities in the 
developing countries about freedom to utilize these flexibilities. The Indian 
Pharmaceutical industry would also benefit in catering to the demand generated 
by authrization of parallel import and compulsory license.

504. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of

(a) whether the Industrial growth in^the country during the past few 
months have reached an alarming point in comparison to the previous year's

440 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government propose to formulate any policy to boost its 
industrial growth rate in the next few months; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) and (b) As per the latest data, 
available, the industrial growth during April-December 2001-02 has been 2.3% 
as against 5.8% registered during the corresponding period of last year. The 
deceleration in industrial growth has been attributable to a number of structural 
and cyclical factors such as: 
• Investment and business cycles. 
• Inherent adjustment lags of corporate restructuring. 
• Lack of both consumer and investment demand. 
• Continued high real interest rates. 
• Infrastructure constraints particularly in power. 
• Delays in establishing credible institutional and regulatory framework 
to provide the requisite comfort level for private participation in some 
key sectors have also dampened private investment and industrial 
production. 
• Lack of reforms in land and labour markets, 
• Continued economic slowdown in countries that are major trading 
partners of India, viz. USA, Japan and European Union. 
(c) and (d) The Government has taken several policy initiatives to boost 
industrial production in the country. These measures have been targeted to 
improve competitiveness of Indian industry in general and to boost aggregate 
demand, improve infrastructure base, upgrade technology, introduce labour 
flexibility and encourage FDI flows. Some of the initiatives taken recently/ 
proposed to be taken are briefly mentioned below: 
• Public spending out of the budgetary allocations has been stepped 
up. Government has already identified several "last mile projects" 
under various ministries for speedy completion. 
441 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
• DIPP has proposed to conduct sector-wise studies in respect of capital 
goods, electrical manufacturing, pulp and paper and cement industries 
with a view to enhance the competitiveness of these industries. 
• Companies Act has been amended to allow buy-back of shares, by 
the companies. 
• To deepen reforms in stock exchanges and to provide protection to 
the investors, Union Budget 2002-03 proposes amendments in SEBI 
Act, 1992. 
• The Government has announced guidelines for allowing 100% FDI 
in the development of integrated townships and regional urban 
infrastructure. This is expected to boost housing/real estate sector 
and also boost production in cement and steel sector. 
• To boost Foreign Institutional Investment (FII) in India, FII portfolio 
investment will not be subject to the Sectoral limits for foreign direct 
investment except in specified sectors 
• Mid term Export strategy for 2002-07 to lay stress on effective tax 
rebate schemes to help exporters. These include transparent and 
comprehensive schemes of reimbursement, comprehensive VAT 
system at every level, rebating service tax besides lower customs 
and excise duties for major inputs needed for exports, which can 
minimise the need for duty drawback. 
• Sector-wise strategies to boost production for exports in key sectors, 
which include engineering / electronic / electrical and allied, textiles, 
gems and jewellery, chemicals and allied sector have also been 
announced. 
• To reduce infrastructure bottlenecks several incentives have been 
announced in the Union Budget 2002-03 for improvement in power, 
roads, civil aviation and ports. 
• The Golden Quadrilateral project will be substantially completed by 
December 2003—a year ahead of schedule, major ports to be 
corporatised in a phased manner and an allocation of Rs. 2500 crore 
has been made for the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Sadak Yojana for 
2002-03. 
• Infrastructure equity fund of Rs. 1000 crore will be set up to help in 
providing equity investment for infrastructure projects. Total Plan outlay 
on infrastructure in power, roads and railway is Rs. 37919 crores. 
442 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
• Union Budget 2002-03 proposes abolition of 16% special excise duty 
on all, except eight items. 
• Additional 15% depreciation on new plant and machinery. 
• Reduction of peak rate of custom duty to 30% rationalisation of custom 
duty rates to two duty rates by 2004-05. 
• Budget 2002-03 announced special incentives for textile industry. 
• Measures to boost Housing sector such as repeal by the States of the 
rules under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, rationalisation of high stamp 
duty regimes proposed in the Union Budget 2002-03.

Down fall in industrial growth 
516. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that industrial growth fell to 2.2% during the first 
eight months of the current financial year as compared to 6% during the same 
period of last fiscal year; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for this drastic downfall and what was the 
anticipated industrial growth for the current financial year; and 
(c) what steps have been taken to ensure that industrial growth maintains 
the anticipated growth pattern during the remaining period? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The decleration in industrial growth has been attributable to a number 
of structural and cyclical factors such as: 
• Investment and business cycles. 
• Inherent adjustment lags of corporate restructuring. 
• Lack of both consumer and investment demand. 
• continued high real interest rates. 
• Infrastructure constraints particularly in power. 
• Delays in establishing crediable institutional and regulatory 
framework to provide the requisite comfort level for private 
participation in some key sectors have also dampened private 
investment and industrial production. 
• Lack of reforms in land and labour markets. 
• Continued economic slowdown in countries that are major trading 
partners of India, viz., USA, Japan, and European Union. 
The Planning Commission has set an annual average target of 8.2% for 
the industrial sector during the Ninth Plan period. The CSO has estimated a 
growth rate of 3.3% during 2001-02 for the manufacturing sector. 
456 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c)The Government has taken several policy initiatives to boost industrial 
production in the country. These measures have been targeted to improve 
competitiveness of Indian industry in general and to boost aggregate demand, 
improve infrastructure base, upgrade te chnology, introduce labour flexibility 
and encourage FDI flows. Some of the initiatives taken recent / proposed to 
be taken are briefly mentioned below: 
• Public spending out of the budgetary allocations has been stepped 
up. Government has already identified several 'last mile projects' 
under various ministries for speedy completion. 
• DIPP has proposed to conduct sector-wise studies in respect of 
capital goods, electrical manufacturing, pulp and paper and cement 
industries with a view to enhance the competitiveness of these 
industries. 
• Companies Act has been amended to allow buy-back of shares, by 
the companies. 
• To deepen reforms in stock exchanges and to provide protection 
to the investors, Union Budget 2002-2003 proposes amendment? 
in SEBI Act 1992. 
• the Government has announced guidelines for allowing 100% FDI 
in the development of integrated townships and regional urban 
infrastructure. This is expected to boost housing / real estate sector 
and also boost production in cement and steel sector. 
• to boost Foreign Institutional Investment (FII) in India, FII portfolio 
investments will not be subject to the Sectoral limits for foreign 
direct investment except in specified sectors. 
• Mid term Export strategy for 2002-07, to lay stress on effective tax 
rebate schemes to help exporters. These include transparent and 
comprehensive schemes of reimbursement, comprehensive VAT 
system at every level, rebating service tax besides lower customs 
and excise duties for major inputs needed for exports, which can 
minimise the need for duty drawback. 
• Sector-wise stragies to boost production for exports in key sectors, which 
include engineering / electronic / electrical and allied, textiles, gems 
and jewellery, chemicals and allied sector have also been announced. 
457 

RAJYA SABHA [7 March, 2002] 
• To reduce infrastructure bottlenecks several incentives have been 
announced in the Union Budget 2002-03 for improvement in power, 
roads, civil aviation and ports. 
• The Golden Quadrilateral project will be substantially completed 
by December 2003-a year ahead of schedule, major ports to be 
corporatised in a phased manner and an allocation of Rs. 2500 
crore has been made for the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Sadak Yojana 
for 2002-03. 
• Infrastructure equity fund of Rs. 1000 crore will be set up to help 
in providing equity investment for infrastructure project. Total Plan 
outlay on infrastructure in power, roads and railway is Rs. 37919 
crores. 
• Union Budget 2002-03 propose abo lition of 16% special excise 
duty on all, except eight items. 
• Additional 15% depreciation on new plant and machinery. 
• Reduction of peak rate of custom duty to 30%, rationalisation of 
custom duty rates to two duty rates by 2004-05. 
• Budget 2002-03 announced special incentives for textile industry. 
• Measures to boost Housing sector such as repeal by the States of 
the rules under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, rationalisation of high 
stamp duty regimes proposed in the Union Budget 2002-03.

537.  SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Banking Service Commission is being 
wound up; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for decentralising the recruitment procedure 
in public sector banks and authorising each bank to recruit directly; and 
(c) the circumstances under which the Banking Service Commission was 
created and what necessitated for dispensing its work? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) Banking Service Commission 
Act, 1984 envisaged setting up of Banking Service Commission for recruitment 
of officers for the Public Sector Banks (PSBs). However, the same has not 
been set up. Hitherto, the Banking Service Recruitment Boards (BSRJBs) set 
up in the year 1978 were making recruitments to various posts for meeting the 
requirements of the public Sector Banks in Clerical / Officers' Cadre. With 
greater emphasis on computerisation and mechanisation and rapidly changing 
economic scenario, the requirement of the banks with regard to their manpower 
has declined and also undergone a change. Banks now require specialized 
officers more in number as compared to the past. Keeping in view the changed 
scenario, BSRBs have been closed down and banks have been advised to 
frame their own recruitment strategy with the approval of their boards to meet 
their future requirements. Banks have further been advised to ensure that 
recruitment policy is transparent, the process of selection is fair, just, objective 
and unbiased and takes care of the reservation policy for SC/ST/OBCs as per 
Government guidelines.

572. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE

(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
which appeared in the "Business Standard" dated the 15th January, 2002

of India; 
(c) if not, what is Government's assessment of the situation thereto; and 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken by Government for boosting output 
and engineering growth? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) to (d) The annual point to point 
inflation rate (based on Wholesale Price Index) remained close to 5 per cent 
level in the first six months of 2001-02 (April-September). It started declining 
only after September to reach a low level of 1.13 per cent in February 2002. 
Low inflation rate may be a manifestation of moving towards a more 
liberalized trade regime. Subdued inflation rate of major trading partner 
496 

[7 March, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
countries are likely to have a bearing on the domestic economy through 
increased competition, influencing to some extent the domestic inflation rate. 
In recent years relatively low inflation rates registered in 1997-98 (4.4 per 
cent) and in 1999-2000 (3.3 per cent) was characterized by relatively high 
industrial growth of 6.7 per cent in both these years.

578. SHRI P.N. SIVA: Will the Mi nister of FINANCE be pleased to

whom cases of corruption by CBI are registered under FR 56 (j);

GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) to (d) Fundamental Rule (FR) 56G)

610. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to introduce an Interest Subsidy 
Scheme for coffee growers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the time by which the scheme is likely 
to be implemented; and 
(c) the details of steps taken by Government to help the coffee growers 
who are facing lots of difficulties, owing to steady decline in prices of coffee? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
Coffee Board is implementing an interest subsidy scheme with an outlay of 
Rs. 4.50 crores, as a pilot project, during the current financial year. The scheme 
provides 5% interest subsidy relief to the targeted small coffee growers on the 
crop / working capital loans availed by them from the financial institutions. 
(c) With the liberalisation of coffee industry, the trade is in the private 
hands and the prices of coffee are determined by the market forces of demand 
and supply. However for the benefit of coffee growers, the Govt, of India through 
Coffee Board has been operating several plan schemes under which various 
types of financial and technical assistance are provided to the growers. Further 
thrust is being given for increasing productivity of coffee particularly in small 
grower sector and improving quality of the product to achieve competitiveness 
in the international market. The Board is also encouraging large growers to 
produce speciality coffee which fetches attractive premium in the developed 
countries. All these steps are expected to stabilize the prices in the long run 
and ensure remunerative return to the growers. 
In addition, at the behest of Govt, of India, the commercial banks 
rescheduled the crop loans of small coffee growers and are also extending 
fresh capital loans to them. The Govt, of India has also approved a 
transportation subsidy scheme to. provide a financial support of Rs. 500 /per 
tone to coffee exporters for reducing the handling costs. 
Coffee Board is also implementing a medium-term export strategy to 
sustain and gain market share in the key markets and also to improve the 
competitiveness of India Coffee in the global market over the next few years.
